key_insight: Capability emergence in language models behaves like a driven nucleation event: all required circuit parts must align together, and missing parts increase the waiting time rather than allowing partial credit.
engineering_relevance: The rate-law framing turns training dynamics into a controllable systems problem, enabling prediction, scheduling, preservation, or suppression of model capabilities by manipulating circuit occupancy and training drive.
method: Derived a stochastic rate equation with terms for sites, attempts, drive, and barrier height, plus a destruction term.
Validated the no-partial-credit mechanism with ablations across Pythia models and multiple capabilities.
Demonstrated control strategies in a gated-attention toy model and via targeted query-key reinitialization.
evidence_signal: Across seven capabilities and three scales, one missing circuit part left only a median 17% of capability in 32/32 discriminating cells, and the proposed kinetics predicted capability onset and delay with strong agreement on held-out models.
watch_item: The rate-law and control results are strongest for conjunction-style circuits, so broader generalization to other capability types or larger frontier models still needs confirmation.
paper_title: The Kinetics of Training: A Driven-Nucleation Rate Law for Emergence, Plasticity Loss, and Circuit Control in Language Models
